newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia poll doubts taint peace process - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia poll doubts taint peace process - diplomats.

text.p: Major discrepancies between the number of voters and ballots counted in Bosnia's elections threaten to undermine the credibility of the whole peace process, according to diplomats and independent observers.
Bosnia held its first post-war national elections on September 14 under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

OSCE has announced preliminary final results for a three-man collective Presidency, a national House of Representatives, separate Serb and Moslem-Croat parliaments, a Serb republic President and cantonal assemblies.

But independent observers maintain hundreds of thousands of bogus ballots were cast or at least counted in an election which currently has Alija Izetbegovic winning the chairmanship of the collective Presidency by a margin of only 41,000 votes.
The International Crisis Group (ICG), a well-regarded independent monitoring group, has filed a formal protest with the OSCE requesting that the entire vote be recounted.
ICG's complaint urges that if the discrepancy between the overall voter population and the number of ballots cast is confirmed, the Bosnian election results should nullified.
"It's scandalous that a week after we asked basic questions about the elections there has still been no response," Hrair Balian, OSCE's legal adviser in Sarajevo, told Reuters.
"It really undermines the credibility of the international effort in Bosnia -- not just for elections but for the entire Dayton peace process."
At the centre of much of the criticism are U.S. government officials charged with certifying the election results.

"I'm afraid the Americans, in their haste to hold the election and pronounce it a success, are beginning to insult the intelligence of even the most dispassionate observer," said a Western diplomat in Sarajevo who asked not to be named.

"They're trying to make a molehill out of a mountain of evidence that substantially more ballots were cast than there were voters to cast them. The outcome in the presidential contest may be very much in doubt. It's becoming a fiasco."
OSCE's head of mission in Bosnia, Robert Frowick, is an American as is its Director General of elections, Jeff Fischer.
All that remains is for Frowick to certify the results after a mandated appeal period expires.
Frowick and Fischer have been unavailable for public comment on the myriad technical issues which preliminary final results have raised.
The OSCE, which two weeks ago had hundreds of high-powered staff swarming across Bosnia, is now so short-handed it has not a single press spokesman to handle enquiries.
"There's been a complete collapse in the information flow from OSCE at the very time when their credibility and the credibility of the elections is most in question," said a U.N. official.
Potentially explosive political problems may await the international community regardless of what is finally decided about the election results.

Izetbegovic, who steered Bosnian Moslems through 43 months of war, has already been anointed by the OSCE as apparent winner in the race for Chairman of the three-man collective presidency, and unseating him now would be awkward.
Bosnian Moslems would be unlikely to accept current second- place finisher Momcilo Krajisnik, a hardline Serb separatist, as the presidency's chairman under any circumstances.

The Serbs have complained about hundreds of thousands of phantom votes and warned that if those ballots are not properly accounted for in the final OSCE tally they may reject the election results altogether.
Looming over the entire process is November's U.S. Presidential election.
Diplomats say the Clinton administration seems determined not to allow the hard-won victory with the Dayton peace agreement it brokered to be sullied by a few hundred thousand questionable ballots.
As one Sarajevo wag put it: "The best the OSCE may be able to do now is to announce that while the winners may have stolen the election, at least they stole it fair and square."
